Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group provides regular supervision and an Annual Performance
and Development Review for every member of staff. It applies to every site and every category of
permanent staff.

Policy statement

Regular supervision and a meaningful Annual Performance and Development Review give every staff
member a structured opportunity to reflect on their practice, raise a concern, and plan their own
development, supporting both individual growth and the quality of care residents receive.

Definitions

**Supervision** a regular one-to-one meeting between a staff member and their line manager, focused on
current practice and immediate support needs. **Annual Performance and Development Review** the
renamed term for what the previous version called an appraisal — the annual, more formal review of a
staff member's overall performance over the past year and their development plan for the year ahead.
**Personal development plan** the agreed set of development actions arising from the Annual
Performance and Development Review.

Roles and responsibilities

**Line managers** conduct supervision at least monthly for every direct report and lead the Annual
Performance and Development Review. **HR** monitors that supervision and the Annual Performance
and Development Review are completed on schedule across all sites. **Staff** come prepared to raise
their own topics in supervision and the review, not only respond to what their manager raises.

1. Conduct supervision with every direct report at least monthly, recorded briefly to note any action agreed.

2. Complete an Annual Performance and Development Review for every staff member annually, covering
performance over the year and a personal development plan for the year ahead; this is the same annual
process previously called an appraisal, renamed in this version.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a staff member is on an extended period of leave spanning their scheduled Annual Performance
and Development Review date, it is completed as soon as practicable after their return rather than skipped
for that year.

Linking the review to career progression

Where a staff member expresses interest in progressing to a more senior role, this is discussed as part of

New manager induction into supervision practice

A newly promoted line manager receives additional coaching on conducting supervision well before taking
on this responsibility for the first time, since giving good supervision is itself a skill that benefits from
support rather than being assumed to come automatically with a management title.

Supervision for an agency or bank worker

A regular agency or bank worker who covers shifts consistently at a site is also offered a lighter-touch
supervision conversation periodically with the shift lead, distinct from the more formal Alderbridge
employment relationship they have with their own agency, since a worker who is a familiar, regular
presence still benefits from the same kind of reflective conversation as a permanent colleague.

Group supervision alongside one-to-one sessions

Some sites also hold an occasional group supervision session covering a shared practice theme relevant
to the whole team, such as a recent change in a care approach, which complements but never replaces
the individual one-to-one supervision each staff member is separately entitled to.

Confidentiality of supervision content

What is discussed in supervision is treated as confidential between the staff member and their line
manager, save where it raises a safeguarding, conduct or safety concern that must be escalated under the
relevant separate policy, and staff are told clearly at the outset where that boundary sits so they can speak

Audit preparation

The auditor samples different times, locations and care interactions and checks prior actions before

confidential records and the physical environment rather than relying on a single general impression.

Evidence and escalation

Findings cite the observed or recorded evidence and distinguish an isolated lapse from a repeated or
systemic concern. Immediate risk, degrading treatment or possible abuse is escalated at once through
safeguarding and management routes; it is not left as a routine audit action. Positive practice is recorded
specifically enough to be repeated elsewhere.

Action and follow-up

Each shortfall receives an accountable owner, due date and completion evidence. The registered manager
reviews the action plan with residents or representatives where appropriate. Follow-up tests whether
practice changed in reality, and overdue or ineffective actions are escalated to the Quality Lead. Audit

Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance

*Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2025. 'Should' becomes 'must' — the buddy assignment is no longer discretionary.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

Extended worked example: a genuinely unsafe address

A worked example illustrates a lone worker exercising the withdrawal right this policy protects. A community support worker arrives at a scheduled visit and finds an unfamiliar, agitated visitor already at the property who was not expected. Rather than proceeding with the visit as planned, the worker withdraws immediately, calls the office from a safe distance, and the office arranges a police welfare check on the client before any further visit is attempted; the incident is logged, the address is flagged for a two-person visit going forward until the situation is better understood, and the worker's decision to withdraw is explicitly praised at the next team meeting as exactly the response this policy expects, not questioned for having left before completing the scheduled care task.

Disciplinary hearings are deliberately held away from the employee's own immediate workplace wherever practicable — for the four care homes and Willow Bank, this typically means using a meeting room at Central Support Office or, where travel is impractical, a private room at a nearby site rather than the employee's own site, to reduce the risk of the hearing itself becoming visible to colleagues or people supported.

A worked example illustrates the boundary between conduct and capability. A relatively new care worker at Riverside House has made three separate documentation errors on care records within two months, none individually serious but forming a pattern. Rather than moving straight to a formal disciplinary hearing, the line manager first considers whether this looks like unwillingness (a conduct matter) or a genuine skills gap (a capability matter) — in this example, the employee's own account and the line manager's review of their induction records show they were never given adequate protected time to complete the documentation training module properly. The line manager therefore addresses this initially through additional supervised practice and a revised, individual learning plan rather than the formal disciplinary process, while recording clearly why that judgement was made, so that if the same pattern continues despite that support, the earlier informal period is not treated as if it never happened.

Time spent driving between community visits is itself a form of lone working, and community support workers are expected to pull over safely before making or taking any call, including a welfare check-in call, rather than attempting to check in while driving; the mobile app's own scheduled check-in windows are set with reasonable travel time built in, so a worker is not placed under pressure to check in at a moment that would require using a phone while still on the road.

New starters and lone working

A new community support worker does not undertake an unaccompanied community visit until they have shadowed an experienced colleague for a minimum of two weeks and completed lone working training, and even after that point, their first fully unaccompanied visits are to addresses already assessed as lower risk, with more complex or previously flagged addresses introduced gradually as the new starter's own confidence and local knowledge builds.

A worked example illustrates a lone worker exercising the withdrawal right this policy protects. A community support worker arrives at a scheduled visit and finds an unfamiliar, agitated visitor already at the property who was not expected.
